Nanocrystalline  cellulose  (NCC),  a  renewable  and  highly  crystalline  natural  polymer,  possesses  a  one-
dimensional nanorod structure, a high specific surface area, and excellent mechanical properties, making it an 
ideal nanofiller for improving the performance of epoxy resin coatings19. Nevertheless, the hydrophilic surface 
of NCC has poor compatibility with lipophilic epoxy resins, thereby limiting its application in epoxy resins20. To 
address the compatibility issue between NCC and epoxy resins, researchers have conducted extensive research. 
These efforts mainly center on the chemical modification of NCC and enhance the dispersibility of NCC in organic 
solvents  and  its  compatibility  with  epoxy  resins  by  introducing  various  functional  groups21,22.  For  instance, 
the surface grafting modification of NCC using modifiers such as n-octadecyl isocyanate, hexanoyl chloride, 
lauroyl  chloride,  and  stearyl  chloride  can  enhance  its  dispersibility  in  organic  solvents  and  its  compatibility 
with the polymer matrix23,24. Additionally, hydrophobic groups and active amino groups can be introduced on 
the  surface  of  NCC  through  the  use  of  silane  coupling  agents  like  γ-(2,3-epoxy)  propyltrimethoxysilane  and 
poly(methylhydrogen)siloxane,  further  strengthening  its  interfacial  interaction  with  epoxy  resin  and  coating 
performance25,26.

Inspired  by  previous  studies,  this  research  utilizes  nanocrystalline  cellulose  (NCC)  as  a  nanofiller  and 
modifies it with an alkoxysilane coupling agent to enhance the compatibility and interfacial adhesion between 
NCC and epoxy resin. By introducing an alkoxysilane coupling agent, hydrophobic groups and active amino 
groups can be introduced on the surface of NCC, thereby improving its dispersibility in organic solvents and 
its  reactivity  with  epoxy  resin.  In  this  study,  the  interface  regulation  mechanism  and  embedding  dispersion 
mechanism of M-NCC and epoxy resin will be systematically explored to construct a metal protective coating 
with outstanding wear resistance, mechanical stability, and hydrophobicity. Simultaneously, the performance of 
the M-NCC/epoxy composite coating in terms of resistance to cold and hot cycles and solvent resistance, as well 
as the corrosion protection effect on Q235 carbon steel, will be evaluated through electrochemical impedance 
spectroscopy,  coating  surface  contact  angle,  and  optical  morphology  analysis.  This  study  aims  to  provide 
theoretical support and practical guidance for the performance improvement of epoxy resin coatings and the 
development of novel anti-corrosion coatings.

Materials and methods
Materials
Sodium  chloride,  DMF,  ethyl  acetate,  anhydrous  ethanol,  3-aminopropyltrimethoxysilane  (APTMS), 
hexadecyltrimethoxysilane  (HDTMS),  aqueous  ammonia  (28%),  epoxy  resin  (E-44)  and  curing  agent  were 
purchased from Aladdin. Q235 carbon steel was purchased from Xincheng Senke Specimen Processing Center. 
NCC was purchased from Northern Century (Jiangsu) Cellulose Material Co., Ltd.

Preparation of M-NCC epoxy solution
1.25 g, 2.5 g, 7.5 g and 12.5 g of NCC solution (with a 2% NCC content) were separately weighed, corresponding 
to absolute dry masses of NCC at 0.025 g, 0.05 g, 0.15 g and 0.25 g, respectively. These were then dispersed in 
anhydrous ethanol. The NCC-ethanol solutions with varying contents were centrifuged at 9000 rpm for 15 min. 
The resulting precipitates were collected and transferred to 30 mL of anhydrous ethanol, and 0.1 g of HDTMS, 
0.05 g of 3 APTMS and 1 mL of ammonia water were added. The NCC was modified under magnetic stirring for 
1 h. Subsequently, 5 g of epoxy resin E-44 was added and stirred for 15 min to yield NCC epoxy solutions with 
mass fractions of 0.5%, 1%, 3% and 5%, respectively (where 0.5%, 1%, 3% and 5% represent the mass ratios of 
the absolute dry NCC to the epoxy resin).

Preparation of M-NCC epoxy coating
The epoxy resin with a mass ratio of epoxy resin E-44 to curing agent of 4 :1 was prepared, and 30 mL ethyl 
acetate was added and stirred evenly. Ethyl acetate was used as a solvent. The epoxy coating primer was prepared 
on pre-polished Q235 carbon steel by the dip-coating method. The thickness of the epoxy coating was 10 ± 2 μm.

M-1% NCC/EP, M-3% NCC/EP, and M-5% NCC/EP coatings. The coating thickness was 75 ± 5 μm.

Preparation of pure epoxy coating
An epoxy-ethyl acetate solution consisting of 5 g epoxy resin E-44 and 30 mL ethyl acetate was sprayed on Q235 
carbon steel with a 10 ± 2 μm epoxy coating and cured at 90  °C for 6 h in an oven to prepare a pure epoxy coating 
with a coating thickness of 75 ± 5 μm.

Electrochemical measurements
A  three-electrode  system  was  employed,  including  a  saturated  calomel  electrode  as  the  reference  electrode, 
a platinum black electrode as the counter electrode, and a Q235 carbon steel electrode with a coating as the 
working  electrode.  EIS  measurements  were  conducted  using  a  Princeton  VersaSTAT  3  F  electrochemical 
workstation with an applied amplitude of 20 mV, a frequency range of 104 ~10− 2, and 10 points per frequency 
doubling. The corrosion process was analyzed by establishing an equivalent circuit diagram and fitting the data 
using the ZView software.

Characterizations
The differences in chemical bonds of the samples were characterized using Fourier Transform Infrared Reflection 
(FTIR, IRPrestige-21) spectroscopy. The TGA and DTG measurements were obtained using a thermogravimetric 
analyzer  (TGA8000)  at  a  heating  rate  of  10  °C  min-1  under  a  nitrogen  atmosphere  (50  mL/min).  FESEM 
(Quanta  FEG  250,  FEI,  USA)  was  employed  to  characterize  the  sample  morphology,  element  content  and 
distribution analysis (EDS and element mapping). X-ray photoelectron spectra (XPS) were acquired using an 
X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (AXIS Ultra DLD, Kratos Co., England), employing monochromatic Al Kα 
radiation (1486.6 eV) as the excitation source. The binding energy was calibrated to 284.6 eV for the C 1s peak. 
The water contact angle (WCA) was measured and calculated on a contact angle measuring instrument (ZJ-
7000, Zhijia Instruments, China) using the dynamic mode, where a drop of 5 µL water was dispensed onto the 
thin film surface by an automatic piston syringe and immediately photographed. The 3D optical topography of 
the samples was measured using a 3D optical profiler (Up S-Dual, RTEC, USA) and visualized using Gwyddion 
software (version 2.44). The optical images of the samples were captured using an optical electronic microscope 
( AO-HD208C, AOSVI, China).

Improvement of anti-swelling 
property and anticorrosion 
performance of epoxy coatings by 
the introduction of nanocrystalline 
cellulose composite

Lei Kang1,2, Qiao Zeng2, Jiang Fan3, Xinzhe Dang1, Hu Chen4, Bo Yan1 & Xingpeng Guo2

In this work, the effect of nanocrystalline cellulose (NCC) as a nanofiller on the corrosion protection 
of epoxy resin coatings was examined. To solve problems like poor solvent swelling resistance and 
micropore formation during the solidification and shrinkage of epoxy resin coatings, NCC was modified 
with a silane coupling agent. Alkyl chains and active amine groups were grafted onto its surface, 
improving the dispersibility of NCC in organic solvents and its bonding with epoxy resin. In this study, 
NCC was modified by hexadecyltrimethoxysilane (HDTMS) and 3-aminopropyltrimethoxysilane 
(APTMS), and the modified NCC (M-NCC) was added to epoxy resin E-44 through dip-coating and 
spraying to prepare M-NCC/EP coatings. The experiments showed that more M-NCC significantly 
enhanced the solvent resistance of the coatings, reducing swelling and peeling in ethyl acetate and 
N, N-dimethylformamide (DMF). The impedance changes of different M-NCC/EP coatings after hot/
cold cycles in 3.5% NaCl solution and air were monitored by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. 
It was found that at 1% and 3% M-NCC doping, the impedance remained high after 60 hot/cold cycles 
in sodium chloride solution and air, indicating excellent protection for carbon steel. The low thermal 
expansion coefficient of NCC and its bond with epoxy resin reduced the internal stress during hot/cold 
cycles. Also, the hydrophobicity of the coating and the filled M-NCC blocked the invasion of corrosive 
media. This study offers new ideas and methods for making high-performance metal protective 
coatings and has significant application value.

Keywords  Nanocrystalline cellulose, Epoxy resin, Corrosion protection, Solvent resistance, Electrochemical 
impedance spectroscopy

Metal corrosion has long been a stubborn and widespread problem in the industrial domain. Particularly in 
extreme conditions marked by high temperatures, high humidity, and high salinity, the corrosion rate of metal 
materials escalates significantly, posing substantial threats to the safe operation of equipment and structures1,2. 
E Epoxy resin coatings, commonly employed as a protective material for metals, offer superior adhesion and 
electrical insulation properties. However, their protective efficacy is often undermined in extremely corrosive 
environments3,  especially  for  metal  hot-end  components  like  those  in  marine  engines  (Liu  et  al.4.  These 
components  are  exposed  to  alternating  high  and  low  temperatures  in  a  marine  salt  spray  environment  over 
prolonged periods5, causing the coatings to age and crack, which subsequently leads to the corrosion of the metal 
substrate6. Thus, enhancing the anti-corrosion performance of epoxy resin coatings under extreme conditions is 
crucial for prolonging the service life of metal materials.

In  extreme  corrosive  settings,  the  performance  of  epoxy  resin  coatings  deteriorates  markedly  due  to  the 
combined influence of multiple factors7–10. These include lapses in the construction process, drastic temperature 
fluctuations in the environment, frequent humidity alterations, intense chemical corrosion, inevitable physical 
shock  damage,  and  the  aging  of  the  material  itself.  These  factors  collectively  act  on  the  coating,  resulting  in

between the coating and the metal substrate. As these defects and stresses persist and worsen, the protective 
performance  of  the  coating  is  severely  weakened,  eventually  leading  to  coating  failure  and  accelerating  the 
corrosion of the metal substrate. Nanofillers have demonstrated a considerable impact on enhancing coating 
performance due to their distinctive size and surface effects. The introduction of nanofillers can effectively fill 
the micropores and cracks within the coating, significantly reduce the permeability of the corrosive medium, 
and notably enhance the interfacial bonding between the coating and the metal substrate, thereby minimizing 
the generation of interfacial stress. Specifically, carbon-based nanofillers like graphene and carbon nanotubes

Metal-based nanofillers, particularly silver nanoparticles, exhibit excellent performance in preventing microbial-
induced  corrosion  due  to  their  outstanding  antibacterial  properties13,12.  Polymer-based  nanofillers,  such  as 
polytetrafluoroethylene  nanoparticles,  can  significantly  enhance  the  hydrophobicity  and  chemical  corrosion 
resistance  of  coatings,  ensuring  their  stability  in  diverse  chemical  environments14,15.  Despite  the  numerous 
benefits brought by nanofiller grafting to coating performance, we must also confront the challenges it poses in 
practical applications. Issues such as the dispersibility and stability of nanofillers, along with their compatibility

research  focuses  is  to  identify  more  suitable  nanofillers,  optimize  the  filler  addition  amount  and  dispersion 
method, and deeply investigate the interaction mechanism between nanofillers and the epoxy resin matrix to 
overcome these challenges and further enhance the performance of coatings.

Preparation of M-NCC epoxy solution
1.25 g, 2.5 g, 7.5 g and 12.5 g of NCC solution (with a 2% NCC content) were separately weighed, corresponding 
to absolute dry masses of NCC at 0.025 g, 0.05 g, 0.15 g and 0.25 g, respectively. These were then dispersed in 
anhydrous ethanol. The NCC-ethanol solutions with varying contents were centrifuged at 9000 rpm for 15 min. 
The resulting precipitates were collected and transferred to 30 mL of anhydrous ethanol, and 0.1 g of HDTMS, 
0.05 g of 3 APTMS and 1 mL of ammonia water were added. The NCC was modified under magnetic stirring for 
1 h. Subsequently, 5 g of epoxy resin E-44 was added and stirred for 15 min to yield NCC epoxy solutions with 
mass fractions of 0.5%, 1%, 3% and 5%, respectively (where 0.5%, 1%, 3% and 5% represent the mass ratios of 
the absolute dry NCC to the epoxy resin).

Preparation of M-NCC epoxy coating
The epoxy resin with a mass ratio of epoxy resin E-44 to curing agent of 4 :1 was prepared, and 30 mL ethyl 
acetate was added and stirred evenly. Ethyl acetate was used as a solvent. The epoxy coating primer was prepared 
on pre-polished Q235 carbon steel by the dip-coating method. The thickness of the epoxy coating was 10 ± 2 μm.

Results and discussion
Characterization of M-NCC epoxy coating
Figure 1a shows the ATR-FTIR spectra of M-NCC and pure NCC with different contents. The M-NCC showed 
two medium-intensity absorption peaks of -NH2 at 3360 cm–1 and 3200 cm–1. The introduction of amino groups 
was the grafting of APTMS in NCC, and the presence of amino groups can provide groups for the ring-opening 
reaction in epoxy resin. A C-H extensional vibration peak was observed at 2901 cm–1, while the Si-O-C and 
Si-O-Si absorption peaks were observed at 1194 cm–1 and 1095 cm–1, respectively, indicating that APTMS and 
HDTMS were successfully grafted onto NCC. In the ATR-FTIR spectrum of pure epoxy resin, characteristic 
absorption  peaks  of  epoxy  groups  and  C-O-C  groups  were  observed  at  916  cm–1  and  1185  cm–1  (as  shown 
in  Fig.  1b).  Upon  addition  of  M-NCC,  these  two  absorption  peaks  were  observed  to  weaken  or  disappear, 
suggesting that the M-NCC underwent a ring-opening reaction in epoxy resin.

The TGA curves of the epoxy coating and the M-3% NCC/EP coating in Fig. 1c show that both coatings 
gradually  lose  weight  at  50 ~ 160  °C  due  to  the  evaporation  of  absorbed  moisture.  Between  200    °C  and  300  
°C,  the  weight-loss  rate  of  the  M-3%  NCC/EP  coating  was  slower  than  that  of  the  epoxy  coating  due  to  the 
presence of a Si-C bond in the M-NCC doped with epoxy resin. This bond has a high bonding energy, which 
delays thermal decomposition. Above 300 °C, the epoxy resin decomposed more rapidly, while the M-3% NCC/
EP coating promoted the formation of silicon carbide and SiO2 at high temperature27, thereby enhancing the 
thermal stability of the coating. Furthermore, the DTG curve (Fig. 1d) shows that the degradation temperature 
of the M-3% NCC/EP coating is higher than that of the pure epoxy coating, suggesting that the M-3% NCC/
EP  coating  has  better  thermal  stability.  Upon  comparison  of  the  residual  weights  of  the  two  coatings  after 
thermogravimetric analysis, it was observed that the residual amount of the coating with M-3% NCC/EP added 
was  greater  than  that  of  the  pure  epoxy  coating. This  was  attributed  to  the  flame-retardant  properties  of  the 
silanized NCC, which generated the volatile products during the decomposition process that acted as a mass 
transfer barrier to prevent thermal decomposition28.

Figure 2 shows the SEM images, EDS and mapping results of pure epoxy coating and M-3% NCC/EP coating. 
The  epoxy  resin  was  coated  onto  the  polished  and  dried  Q235  carbon  steel,  and  the  resulting  epoxy  coating 
exhibited a smooth surface without obvious particles (Fig. 2a). In the EDS and mapping test results (Fig. 2b and 
c), the C, O, N and Si elements were identified and evenly distributed. The detected Si element may originate 
from impurities in the raw materials. The main components of the epoxy resin are C and O elements, while the 
N element is derived from amine curing agents. The surface morphology of the coating after adding modified 
3% NCC/EP is shown in Fig. 2c. Compared with the pure epoxy coating, the surface roughness of the M-3% 
NCC/EP coating increased, with rod-like and granular morphologies observed on the surface. NCC is a rod-like 
structure. After modification, siloxane chains were grafted on the surface, leading to an increase in the volume 
of NCC, which appeared as particles or rods in the epoxy coating. Four elements, including C, N, O, and Si, were 
identified by EDS and mapping. The significant increase in the proportion of N and C elements can be attributed 
to the HDTMS and APTMS reagents used in the modification of the added NCC.

Wettability of M-NCC epoxy coating
Pure EP coating is inherently hydrophilic, as evidenced by its low WCA of 65.7° (Fig. 4a). When unmodified 
NCC (a hydrophilic material) is added alone, the WCA slightly decreases to 62.9° (Fig. 4b), consistent with the 
hydrophilic nature of both components. In contrast (Fig. 4c), the introduction of hydrophobic RSiO into EP 
improves hydrophobicity, increasing the WCA to 94.1°—this is attributed to the incorporation of hydrophobic 
functional groups from RSiO, which reduce surface affinity for water.

The M-NCC (functionalized with RSiO) combines the hydrophobicity of RSiO with the ability to introduce 
nanoscale  roughness.  At  a  low  loading  of  0.5%,  the  M-NCC  disperses  uniformly,  creating  micro/nanoscale 
protrusions  on  the  coating  surface.  According  to  the  Cassie-Baxter  principle,  this  roughness  amplifies  the 
hydrophobic effect of the RSiO component: water droplets are partially supported by air pockets trapped in the 
rough structure, reducing contact with the solid surface and increasing the WCA to 100.9°—a value higher than 
that of EP + RSiO (94.1°), which lacks such roughness.

As  the  content  of  M-NCC  increases  (Fig.  4e–g),  the  surface  roughness  further  intensifies  due  to  the 
accumulation  of  more  nanoscale  particles.  This  leads  to  a  gradual  increase  in  WCA,  reaching  107.4°  at  5% 
loading, as the enhanced roughness continues to synergize with the hydrophobic surface chemistry. This trend

When the epoxy coating was subjected to cyclic heating in air from 100 °C to 25 °C, the impedance modulus

decrease after 60 cycles. This is attributed to the fact that NCC has a low thermal expansion coefficient, and

internal stress of the coating induced by alternating high and low temperatures, reduce the damage caused by 
coating cracks due to internal stress, and thus enhancing the protective performance of the coating in a thermal

The results of the EIS tests showed that after 60 cycles of high and low temperatures in 3.5% NaCl solution and 
in air, the M-NCC composite epoxy coating exhibited better protective performance than pure organic epoxy 
coating. In particular, when the addition amount of M-NCC was 1% and 3%, the protective effect of the coating 
was the most significant. This was mainly due to the low expansion coefficient of NCC and the close bonding 
between M-NCC and epoxy resin through chemical bonds, which effectively reduced the thermal expansion and 
internal stress of epoxy resin during thermal cycling. In addition, the hydrophobicity of the M-NCC/EP coating 
and the filled M-NCC contributed to blocking the invasion of corrosive media, further enhancing the protective 
performance of the coating.

To  sum  up,  this  study  successfully  developed  a  M-NCC/epoxy  composite  coating  with  excellent  solvent 
resistance, corrosion resistance and thermal cycling resistance by utilizing green and environmentally friendly 
nanocrystalline  cellulose  and  a  silane  coupling  agent  with  low  production  cost.  This  achievement  not  only 
provides a new strategy for enhancing the performance of epoxy coatings, but also offers an important theoretical 
and practical basis for expanding their application in extreme environments.
